title: networking-streaming-overhead-benchmarks
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures experiments, measurements, and early conclusions from benchmarking networking and streaming overheads in the serving runtime. Focus areas: HTTP vs gRPC, chunking strategies, client/server backpressure behavior, and common proxy interaction patterns. Goal is to produce actionable recommendations for default transport configuration and runtime knobs that minimize per-token latency and CPU overhead while preserving reliability.

Summary (TL;DR):
- gRPC streaming had lower median per-token overhead than HTTP streaming for stable long-lived connections (5-12% improvement in our setup), but HTTP/2-based gRPC saw larger tail improvements only when connection reuse is ensured.
- Small chunk sizes (<=512 bytes) increase CPU and serialization overhead; ideal chunking depends on model throughput: for low-qps interactive requests prefer 1KB-4KB chunks, for high-throughput batching larger chunks up to 16KB reduce syscalls and proxy overhead.
- Backpressure semantics differ: our HTTP streaming path showed buffer accumulation at proxies leading to 100-300ms added tail under bursty patterns; gRPC flow control maps more cleanly to socket-level backpressure and had fewer proxy-induced tails.
- Sidecar/proxy (Envoy) config matters: defaults can add ~0.5ms-2ms per-chunk overhead; tuning buffer limits and stream window sizes reduced tail latencies significantly.

Testbed and methodology:
- Hardware: dedicated serving node (8x A100, 512GB RAM) running runtime v0.9-prod; client machines: 3x c6i.large-equivalent instances generating traffic.
- Network: 10Gbps private VLAN with single hop; a separate proxy host running Envoy v1.29 used for proxy tests.
- Models: small lm (7B), medium chat (13B), all tests use identical tokenization and prompt seeds.
- Workloads:
  - Interactive: 100 concurrent clients, 1-2 reqs/s per client, variable output lengths (8-256 tokens).
  - Streaming long outputs: 10 concurrent clients, sustained 200 token outputs, high-pipeline of token emission.
  - High-throughput batching: 200 qps with batched responses of 32 items.
- Transports tested: HTTP/1.1 chunked, HTTP/2 streaming (server-sent), gRPC bidirectional streaming.
- Metrics captured: per-token latency, end-to-end request latency, CPU usage (user/sys), syscalls (write/send), context switches, socket buffer fill ratios, Envoy per-request processing time.
- Profiling tools: eBPF tracepoints for network syscalls, perf on runtime worker threads, Envoy stats, tcpdump for validating chunk boundaries.

Key experiments and results:
1) HTTP/1.1 chunked vs gRPC streaming (no proxy)
   - Setup: direct client->runtime, 1KB chunks, interactive workload.
   - Observations:
     - Median per-token latency: HTTP/1.1 = 6.2ms, gRPC = 5.6ms (10% improvement).
     - 95th percentile: HTTP/1.1 = 28ms, gRPC = 24ms.
     - CPU: HTTP path incurred ~7% higher user CPU due to repeated chunk framing and header processing in our HTTP stack.
     - Syscalls: HTTP showed ~18% more send() syscalls per token due to smaller effective writes.
   - Notes: gRPC benefits primarily from HTTP/2 connection multiplexing and fewer per-message framing overheads.

2) Chunk size sweep (HTTP/2 + gRPC)
   - Sweeped chunk sizes: 256B, 512B, 1KB, 4KB, 16KB.
   - Findings:
     - Very small chunks (<=512B) increase CPU/syscall overhead; tail latencies increased by 12-30% under bursty arrival patterns.
     - 1KB-4KB balanced latency and efficiency for interactive workloads; 16KB gave best CPU efficiency but increased tail when proxies applied because of head-of-line blocking in some proxy configs.

3) Backpressure and flow-control behavior (Envoy proxy in path)
   - Observations:
     - Default Envoy buffered up to 64KB per stream which allowed bursts to accumulate and then be drained causing 100-300ms tail spikes for downstream clients.
     - gRPC streaming benefits from HTTP/2 flow control WINDOW_UPDATE semantics; when Envoy window sizes are aligned with our chunking strategy tails reduce.
     - When runtime applied internal buffering (KV/prefix caches) without feedback to transport, end-to-end latency degraded under bursts; we need to surface backpressure signals (TCP-level or flow control) to application queueing layer.

4) Proxy CPU overhead and per-chunk cost
   - Envoy added ~0.4-1.8ms per chunk in our tests depending on filter chain (L7 filters increased cost). This is additive to runtime emission latency and becomes significant for small chunk sizes.

Practical recommendations (initial):
- Default transport: gRPC streaming (HTTP/2) for hosted and dedicated deployments where long-lived connections and connection reuse are expected. Falls back to HTTP/1.1 chunked only for clients/environments without HTTP/2 support.
- Chunking defaults:
  - Interactive: default chunk target 2KB (min 1KB, max 4KB).
  - High-throughput batching: larger chunking up to 16KB allowed; expose config knob per route.
- Backpressure controls:
  - Surface TCP/H2 window events to the runtime's request emission module; implement backpressure-aware token emission to avoid internal buffer buildup.
  - For environments using Envoy, recommend tuning per-stream buffer limits to 16KB-64KB and increase H2 initial window size to match chunking strategy. Document example Envoy config in runbook.
- Proxy filter chain: keep filter chain minimal on streaming routes. Offload heavier L7 processing to a separate non-streaming route when possible.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Need to validate these results across cloud providers and inter-region links (added latency+varied MTU). Tests above were single-region private VLAN.
- Quantize impact for very large models where token emission intervals are longer — overhead fraction may be negligible; re-run with 70B+ models.
- Evaluate WebSocket streaming path (for browser clients) vs HTTP/gRPC tradeoffs (we saw early signs that WS can be competitive with careful chunking but needs more tests).

Notes / rough traces (raw) - include as appendices in final doc:
- eBPF syscall trace snippet (abbreviated):
  - sendto(udp) style not used; tcp send() syscalls per-chunk: HTTP: 12k/sec, gRPC: 9.8k/sec under test workload.
- Sample Envoy stat excerpt:
  - upstream_rq_active: 312
  - http2.tx_flush_time_ms_bucket: [counts] shows tail concentration at 200-300ms under default config.

Appendix: example Envoy tuning snippet (high level, for runbook)
- Per-route config suggestions:
  - http2: max-concurrent-streams: 1000
  - per-stream buffer limit: 65536
  - initial_stream_window_size: 131072
  - connection buffer limits: set to avoid head-of-line for small-chunk interleaving
